stories.title: Trump could discuss 'tacit' N.K. nuke acceptance, peace treaty, allied drills with Kim in possible summit: ex-official

article_sentences: U.S. President Donald Trump could put on the table the "tacit" acceptance of North Korea's nuclear program, a peace treaty and an end to South Korea-U.S. military exercises should a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un take place, a former U.S. official has said.

Anthony Ruggiero, who served as the National Security Council's (NSC) director for North Korea during the first Trump administration," made the comment in an opinion piece published by The Hill, a U.S. media outlet, on Thursday as Trump recently expressed his intention to meet Kim later this year.

Speculation has continued that Trump could seek a meeting with Kim during his next trip to Asia, likely to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, as The Wall Street Journal recently reported.
"Negotiations with Kim will likely include at least a tacit acknowledgement of North Korea's nuclear weapons program," he said.

Ruggiero went on to say, "In addition to Washington's acceptance of North Korea's nuclear program, Trump could offer a peace treaty formally ending the Korean War, a better political and economic relationship, and a permanent end to military exercises with South Korea."
He added that Trump could also facilitate future negotiations between the two Koreas.

As Trump intends to rekindle his personal diplomacy with Kim, concerns have arisen that he could take a more practical approach to the North, shifting Washington's policy focus to goals short of denuclearization, such as arms control or tension reduction.

Those concerns were recently reinforced as Trump revealed that Pyongyang has 57 "very powerful" nuclear weapons, and declined to answer a question about whether his goal in his potential reengagement with Kim remains denuclearization.
Apparently mindful of those concerns, the State Department on Wednesday reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to the "complete" denuclearization of North Korea.
A U.S. official also said separately that there has been "no change" in U.S. policy toward Pyongyang.

In the opinion piece, Ruggiero underscored the need for Trump to insist on "verifiable" limits on Pyongyang's long-range ballistic missile and nuclear weapons programs should a meeting with Kim resume.
Any deal would also need to include North Korea withdrawing all troops and military assistance for Russia's war in Ukraine, he said.
